title: Trách nhiệm cá nhân và điều trị · Advantages / Disadvantages
prompt: In some societies, charging higher public healthcare fees to people whose illnesses are linked to lifestyle choices is being considered. Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

paragraphs: Higher treatment charges assume that responsibility for illness can be separated neatly from addiction and living conditions. I oppose higher public treatment fees for lifestyle-related illness because they can deter care without giving disadvantaged patients a realistic way to change. On balance, the disadvantages are greater in the unrestricted form proposed.

Personal contributions may encourage some people to consider preventable health risks. A visible financial consequence can make the costs of repeated harmful behaviour harder to ignore. A smoker offered accessible cessation support might reconsider a costly habit. That incentive is most plausible where cessation support makes change achievable; a financial threat alone may have limited force against dependency or constrained living conditions. Charging more may discourage timely treatment among people with the fewest resources, even when their illness is partly associated with behaviour.

Lifestyle is shaped by income, addiction and living conditions, so charging can punish disadvantage. Additional charges can make people postpone appointments rather than change an addictive behaviour. Illness may then become more serious and costly to treat, while clinicians face the difficult task of separating personal choice from income, environment and other causes. Public treatment should remain accessible while prevention addresses the conditions behind harmful choices. Keeping treatment accessible avoids punishing delayed presentation, while support for prevention can address risk without requiring clinicians to assign a simplistic share of personal blame. I would favour accessible prevention over punitive treatment fees, because accountability must be balanced against addiction, constrained choices and the consequences of delayed care. A possible incentive to quit is outweighed by delayed care and the difficulty of assigning personal blame for illnesses with several interacting causes.
Accessible treatment and practical prevention offer a fairer response than punitive fees, which can make illness worse precisely among patients least able to afford timely help.
